arc_intro:
FQ-156 — Priya Nair (Cloud Architect)

Time to wire this properly. Right now foodquick-orders-db sits in a private subnet with a route table that has no internet route at all — not even outbound. That's fine for a database that only talks to the app tier. But it won't be fine the moment anything in a private subnet needs to reach the internet — a package update, an external payment API, anything.

We need a real NAT Gateway, wired correctly, and I want you to actually understand why it has to sit where it does — this is one people get backwards constantly.

Also — while you're in the route tables, take another look at that 10.50.0.0/16 entry. I pulled some traffic logs out of curiosity. Tell me what you see.

— Priya
arc_outro:
Priya Nair — FQ-156 update:

NAT Gateway's live, correctly placed, correctly routed — private subnet resources can reach the internet outbound now, and nothing can reach them unsolicited from outside. That part's done right.

The flow logs you found are the real news here. Something in this account tried to reach 10.50.13.4 four times in the last six weeks — a specific address inside that mystery 10.50.0.0/16 range, not just random noise. That's not an old, dead artifact anymore. Something in FoodQuick's infrastructure is STILL actively trying to talk to whatever used to be on the other end of that peering connection. I want to know what's making that call before we do anything else with this route.

Next: security groups and NACLs. We've been leaning on security groups this whole time — let's understand where they stop being enough.

— Priya

tasks.question: How is an Internet Gateway (IGW) different from a NAT Gateway, in terms of the direction traffic can flow?
options: A) They're functionally identical — IGW is just the older name for the same feature

B) An IGW allows traffic BOTH ways (inbound and outbound) — this is why resources in a public subnet can be reached directly from the internet. A NAT Gateway only allows OUTBOUND-initiated traffic — resources behind it can reach the internet, but nothing on the internet can initiate a connection TO them
C) An IGW is outbound-only, and a NAT Gateway is bidirectional — the reverse of the real behavior
D) Both are outbound-only; neither ever allows inbound connections

tasks.question: A NAT Gateway's entire job is to give PRIVATE subnet resources outbound internet access. Given that, which subnet should the NAT Gateway itself actually be created in?
options: A) The same private subnet it's serving — that way it's close to the resources that need it

B) A PUBLIC subnet — the NAT Gateway itself needs its own route to an Internet Gateway to reach the internet on behalf of the private subnet; if it were placed in a private subnet, it would have no internet access itself and couldn't do its job
C) It doesn't matter which subnet, since NAT Gateways aren't actually placed inside any specific subnet
D) A completely separate VPC dedicated only to NAT Gateways

tasks.scenario: Priya asks for a recommendation on NAT Gateway redundancy: should FoodQuick use one shared NAT Gateway for all 3 AZs, or one NAT Gateway per AZ?
options: A) One shared NAT Gateway is always sufficient — NAT Gateways are inherently multi-AZ by design

B) One NAT Gateway PER AZ, with each AZ's private subnets routing to the NAT Gateway in their OWN AZ — this avoids cross-AZ data transfer charges and means losing one AZ doesn't take down outbound internet access for the other AZs' private subnets too
C) No NAT Gateway should ever be used — private subnets should just be given public IPs instead when they need internet access
D) A single NAT Gateway shared across AZs is fine for cost, and the cross-AZ risk doesn't matter since NAT Gateways never fail

tasks.scenario: Ravi flags NAT Gateway costs in the monthly AWS bill review — they're higher than he expected. A NAT Gateway costs roughly ₹2.80/hour (~₹2,000/month) just to exist, PLUS roughly ₹3.20 per GB of data processed through it — separate from any data transfer charges. FoodQuick's private-subnet workloads currently process about 400GB/month through the NAT Gateway.
tasks.question: What's the actual monthly cost breakdown, and is 3 NAT Gateways (one per AZ, per the redundancy recommendation) proportionally reasonable?
tasks.solution: Per NAT Gateway: ~₹2,000/month base + (400GB × ₹3.20 ≈ ₹1,280/month data processing) ≈ ₹3,280/month per gateway if all traffic ran through one. Spread across 3 NAT Gateways (one per AZ), the ₹2,000 base cost triples to ~₹6,000/month, while the ~₹1,280 data processing cost gets split across the 3 based on which AZ's traffic uses which gateway — total data cost stays roughly the same (~₹1,280/month combined), it's just distributed. Total for 3 NAT Gateways: roughly ₹7,280/month, versus ~₹3,280/month for a single shared one — an extra ~₹4,000/month for AZ-level resilience. Reasonable, given a single shared NAT Gateway failing takes down outbound access for the entire VPC's private subnets at once.
tasks.explanation: NAT Gateway's cost 2 parts — fixed hourly cost + per-GB data processing cost, both koodadai real bill will come. 3 NAT Gateways — base cost multiply will happen, but resilience's real value's in opposite paathu, reasonable trade-off.
